mcqs.q: Extraction is defined as the removal of the tooth from:
opts: The alveolus in the alveolar bone
The basal bone of the jaw
mcqs.explain: It is the most common minor surgical procedure performed by the dental professional, combining principles of surgery with principles of physics and mechanics.

mcqs.q: Extraction for pulpal necrosis is considered when:
opts: The patient refuses endodontics, or endodontics cannot be done for technical reasons
The tooth is merely sensitive to cold
The tooth has a small occlusal restoration
mcqs.explain: Pulp necrosis follows irreversible pulpitis; failed endodontic treatment is also an indication for extraction.

mcqs.q: In severe periodontal disease, extraction is indicated because:
opts: Bone loss causes irreversible mobility so the tooth cannot take masticatory load
mcqs.explain: Loss of bone support causes irreversible mobility and pain under normal masticatory load, so the tooth cannot support mastication.

mcqs.q: Before removing an over-retained deciduous tooth you should FIRST:
opts: Take a radiograph to assess the remaining structure and proximity to the permanent tooth/bud
mcqs.explain: The radiograph shows how much deciduous tooth remains and its relation to the erupting permanent tooth or its bud.

mcqs.q: Which is an ORTHODONTIC indication for extraction?
opts: Intentional removal of premolars to gain space for crowding
Removal of a tooth in a fracture line
Removal of a tooth involved by a cyst
Removal of an unrestorable carious tooth
mcqs.explain: Premolars are commonly removed to gain space; erupting third molars may also be removed for their role in crowding.

mcqs.q: A tooth becomes impacted because of all the following EXCEPT:
opts: Dense overlying bone or excessive overlying soft tissue
mcqs.explain: An impacted tooth fails to erupt to its functional level within the expected time due to inadequate space, obstruction, dense bone or excessive soft tissue.

mcqs.q: The pathology most commonly developing around an impacted tooth is a:
mcqs.explain: Impacted teeth are removed for constant pressure on the adjacent tooth, pericoronitis from food lodgment, development of pathology (commonly a dentigerous cyst) and crowding.

mcqs.q: Which is an ABSOLUTE local contraindication to extraction?
opts: Haemangioma or arteriovenous malformation adjacent to the tooth
mcqs.explain: Extraction adjacent to a vascular malformation can cause uncontrolled bleeding and even death — it is never done. The others are relative contraindications.

mcqs.q: A patient presents with an acute dental abscess and cellulitis. The correct approach is to:
opts: Subside the infection with antibiotic therapy, then extract
mcqs.explain: Acute infection is a RELATIVE local contraindication — extraction can be done after modification (settling the infection first).

mcqs.q: Extraction of a tooth in an irradiated jaw may lead to:
mcqs.explain: Extraction should be performed BEFORE radiotherapy, or after 6 months of radiation therapy.

mcqs.q: Extraction should be performed before radiotherapy or after:
mcqs.explain: This timing minimises the risk of osteoradionecrosis in the irradiated field.

mcqs.q: A tooth immediately adjacent to a malignant tumour should be extracted:
opts: At the time of surgical resection, because of the risk of metastasis
mcqs.explain: Extracting such a tooth separately risks distant spread (metastasis), so it is done at the time of surgical resection.

mcqs.q: Local anaesthesia abolishes pain, temperature and touch, but does NOT anaesthetise:
mcqs.explain: Because proprioception persists, the patient must be educated about the difference between pain and pressure.

mcqs.q: When anaesthetising a MAXILLARY tooth for extraction, the surgeon should also anaesthetise the adjacent tooth because:
opts: The adjacent tooth is subjected to pressure the patient may feel as pain
The adjacent tooth will also be extracted
It reduces the total anaesthetic dose
mcqs.explain: During the extraction process the adjacent tooth experiences pressure which the patient may interpret as pain.

mcqs.q: A patient still has sharp pain on luxation despite profound soft-tissue and pulpal anaesthesia. The appropriate step is a:
opts: Second inferior alveolar nerve block only
mcqs.explain: This is likely when the tooth has pulpitis or the surrounding bone is inflamed; a PDL supplementary injection is indicated.

mcqs.q: Bupivacaine may be selected for a traumatic extraction because it provides:
mcqs.explain: A long-acting local anaesthetic is used for post-operative pain control when the procedure is traumatic.

mcqs.q: Which is a PHARMACOLOGICAL method of anxiety control?
opts: Expression of empathy by the dentist
mcqs.explain: Pharmacological methods include oral drugs such as diazepam, nitrous oxide inhalation and intravenous drugs for deep sedation; the others are non-pharmacological.

mcqs.q: Which factor is listed as increasing patient anxiety during extraction?
opts: Clicking of instruments and cracking of bone/tooth
The colour of the operatory walls
mcqs.explain: Anxiety is increased by fear of pain, previous experience, experiences of friends/relatives, instrument clicking, cracking of bone or tooth, and psychological aspects.

mcqs.q: In clinical evaluation, trismus and TMJ dysfunction primarily affect:
opts: Access to the tooth (restricted mouth opening)
mcqs.explain: Restricted opening makes adaptation of forceps and elevators difficult; position of the tooth and crowding also affect access.

mcqs.q: A NON-MOBILE tooth should be carefully evaluated for:
mcqs.explain: Mobile teeth are always easy to extract; a non-mobile tooth may be ankylosed or hypercementosed, posing difficulty.

mcqs.q: A non-vital tooth is more likely to fracture during extraction because it is:
mcqs.explain: Extensive caries, large restorations and non-vitality all predispose the crown to fracture when held with forceps.

mcqs.q: Which radiograph gives the MOST detail before a simple extraction?
mcqs.explain: Periapical films give more detail; panoramic films are useful during removal of impacted teeth.

mcqs.q: Radiographs older than which period should be avoided before extraction?
mcqs.explain: A recent film is needed to depict the current situation around the tooth.

mcqs.q: Assessing the relation of maxillary molars to the maxillary sinus warns of:
opts: Oro-antral communication and displacement of a root fragment into the sinus
Injury to the inferior alveolar bundle
mcqs.explain: Proximity of mandibular molars to the inferior alveolar canal risks neurovascular injury, and premolars near the mental foramen risk mental nerve injury.

mcqs.q: Which root configuration is EASIEST to extract?
mcqs.explain: Long, severely curved, hypercementosed, resorbed or endodontically treated (brittle) roots all increase difficulty and fracture risk.

mcqs.q: Hypercementosis is most commonly found in:
mcqs.explain: It is common in elderly patients, is difficult to extract and carries a chance of bone fracture.

mcqs.q: Regarding bone density on the radiograph:
opts: A tooth surrounded by radiolucent bone is easier to extract than one in radiodense bone
mcqs.explain: Radiolucent (less dense) bone yields more easily; surrounding bone should also be checked for cysts or granulomas, which are removed at the end of the procedure.

mcqs.q: For a MAXILLARY extraction, the patient's mouth should be at the height of the dentist's:
opts: Shoulder, with the occlusal plane at 45° to the horizontal
Elbow, with the occlusal plane parallel to the horizontal
Waist, with the chair fully reclined
mcqs.explain: For mandibular extractions the chair is lower — nearly at elbow level — with the occlusal surface parallel to the horizontal.

mcqs.q: For a MANDIBULAR extraction, the occlusal surface should be:
opts: Parallel to the horizontal, with the chair near the dentist's elbow
At 45° to the horizontal, at shoulder height
mcqs.explain: This positioning gives the operator direct vision and an efficient force vector.

mcqs.q: For extracting the RIGHT mandibular posterior teeth, a right-handed dentist stands:
opts: To the right and behind the patient (10 o'clock)
In front and to the right (7 o'clock)
To the left of the patient
mcqs.explain: For all maxillary teeth and all other mandibular teeth the dentist stands in front and to the right (7 o'clock).

mcqs.q: During extraction, force should be delivered:
opts: From the arm and shoulder, not from the hand alone
By leaning the whole body weight forward
mcqs.explain: A standing, erect posture with weight equally distributed on both legs and controlled force from the arm and shoulder is recommended.

mcqs.q: Which is a role of the operator's OPPOSITE (non-dominant) hand?
opts: Supporting and stabilising the alveolar process around the tooth
mcqs.explain: The opposite hand supports the alveolar process, reflects soft tissue, supports the mandible, protects other teeth, delivers the tooth/root and compresses the socket; holding suction and supporting the head are the assistant's roles.

mcqs.q: Which is a role of the ASSISTANT during extraction?
opts: Holding the suction and protecting the teeth of the opposite arch
Reflecting the soft tissue with the operator's hand
Delivering the tooth from the socket
mcqs.explain: The assistant supports the head and mandible, improves access and visualisation, gives psychological/emotional support, holds suction and protects the opposing teeth.

saqs.q: List the indications for tooth extraction.
saqs.a: Unrestorable caries · pulpal necrosis after irreversible pulpitis when endodontics is refused, impossible or failed · severe periodontal disease · over-retained deciduous teeth · prosthodontic reasons · orthodontic reasons · impacted teeth · supernumerary teeth · fractured crowns or roots · teeth in a fracture line · teeth in cysts or tumours · teeth in a radiotherapy field.

head: Indication
Detail
rows: UNRESTORABLE CARIES
extent and complexity make the tooth non-restorable
PULPAL NECROSIS
after irreversible pulpitis — the patient refuses endodontics, it is technically impossible, or it has failed
SEVERE PERIODONTAL DISEASE
bone loss, irreversible mobility, inability to bear masticatory load
OVER-RETAINED DECIDUOUS TEETH
after radiographic assessment
PROSTHODONTIC
few remaining teeth with a wish for a complete denture · teeth whose position hinders RPD design · teeth unsuitable as abutments
ORTHODONTIC
intentional removal of premolars to relieve crowding · third molars contributing to crowding
IMPACTED TEETH
pressure on adjacent teeth · pericoronitis · pathology such as a dentigerous cyst · crowding
OTHERS
supernumerary teeth · fractured crowns or roots · teeth in the line of a mandibular fracture · teeth in cysts or tumours · teeth in the field of jaw radiotherapy

saqs.q: Classify the contraindications to extraction with examples.
saqs.a: LOCAL ABSOLUTE — haemangioma or AVM adjacent to the tooth; uncontrolled bleeding and even death, so exclude vascular malformations. LOCAL RELATIVE — acute infection (settle first); jaw radiotherapy (osteoradionecrosis — extract before, or after 6 months); teeth adjacent to malignancy (extract at resection). SYSTEMIC RELATIVE — uncontrolled diabetes, bleeding disorders, cardiovascular disorders, long-term steroids, liver disorders, hypertension, pregnancy.

head: Class
Examples
rows:
LOCAL ABSOLUTE
never extract
haemangioma or arteriovenous malformation adjacent to the tooth — the procedure can cause uncontrolled bleeding and even death, so vascular malformations of the jaws must be excluded

LOCAL RELATIVE
possible with modification

acute infection (pericoronitis, abscess, cellulitis) — settle with antibiotics first · radiotherapy to the jaws — risk of osteoradionecrosis, so extract before radiotherapy or after 6 months · teeth adjacent to malignant tumours — risk of metastasis, so extract at the time of surgical resection
SYSTEMIC RELATIVE
uncontrolled diabetes mellitus · bleeding disorders · cardiovascular disorders · long-term steroid therapy · liver disorders · hypertension · pregnancy

saqs.q: Describe the principles of pain and anxiety control for extraction.
saqs.a: PAIN — know the innervation and the maximum LA dose; anaesthetise the adjacent maxillary tooth too; LA abolishes pain, temperature and touch but NOT proprioception, so educate the patient on pain vs pressure; give a PDL injection if sharp pain persists on luxation; bupivacaine gives 6–8 hours. ANXIETY — controlled non-pharmacologically (explanation, assurance, empathy) and pharmacologically (oral diazepam, nitrous oxide, IV deep sedation).

list: Know the correct innervation of the tooth and adjacent structures
Know the maximum recommended dose of local anaesthetic — especially in children and medically compromised patients — calculating it when multiple cartridges are used
Anaesthetise the adjacent maxillary tooth too, since it will feel pressure the patient may perceive as pain
LA abolishes pain, temperature and touch but NOT proprioceptive fibres — educate the patient on the difference between pain and pressure
If sharp pain persists on luxation (likely with pulpitis or inflamed bone), give a periodontal ligament (PDL) supplementary injection
A long-acting agent such as bupivacaine gives 6–8 hours of post-operative effect

head: Increased by
Controlled by
rows: fear of pain · previous experience · others' experiences · instrument clicking · cracking of bone or tooth · psychological factors

Non-pharmacological — explanation, assurance, empathy.
Pharmacological — oral diazepam, nitrous oxide inhalation, intravenous deep sedation

saqs.q: What is assessed in the CLINICAL evaluation of a tooth planned for extraction?
saqs.a: ACCESS — trismus and TMJ dysfunction restrict opening; difficulty adapting forceps and elevators; location and position in the arch; crowded or malposed teeth. MOBILITY — mobile teeth are easy; a non-mobile tooth must be evaluated for ankylosis or hypercementosis. CONDITION OF THE CROWN — extensive caries, non-vital brittle teeth and large restorations all risk fracture, as may an adjacent weak crown.

head: Factor
What is assessed
rows: ACCESS TO THE TOOTH

trismus (spasm of the muscles of mastication) and TMJ dysfunction causing restricted opening · difficulty adapting forceps and elevators · the location and position in the arch (e.g. lingually placed lower premolars) · crowded or malposed teeth
MOBILITY
mobile teeth are always easy to extract; a non-mobile tooth must be evaluated for ankylosis or hypercementosis
CONDITION OF THE CROWN
extensive caries can cause crown fracture when gripped · non-vital teeth are brittle · a large restoration may fracture · an adjacent restored or weak-crowned tooth may also fracture

saqs.q: Outline the radiographic evaluation before extraction.
saqs.a: CRITERIA — periapicals give most detail, panoramics for impactions, avoid films over a year old, note relations to adjacent erupted and unerupted teeth. VITAL STRUCTURES — maxillary sinus, inferior alveolar canal, mental foramen. ROOTS — number, curvature and divergence, hypercementosis, caries and resorption, endodontically treated roots. BONE — radiolucent easy, radiodense difficult; remove surrounding pathology at the end.

head: Area
What to look for
rows: CRITERIA
periapicals give the most detail · panoramics are useful for impacted teeth · avoid films older than one year · note the relationship to adjacent erupted and unerupted teeth
VITAL STRUCTURES

maxillary molars/premolars to the maxillary sinus — difficulty, oro-antral communication, root displacement into the sinus · mandibular molars to the inferior alveolar canal — neurovascular injury · premolars to the mental foramen — mental nerve injury if a flap is raised
ROOT CONFIGURATION

number (extra roots may fracture) · curvature and divergence (short conical roots easier than long severely curved) · hypercementosis (common in the elderly — difficult, risk of bone fracture) · root caries and internal/external resorption (fracture risk) · endodontically treated roots (brittle, sometimes ankylosed)
CONDITION OF BONE
radiolucent bone is easy, radiodense bone difficult; surrounding pathology such as a periapical cyst or granuloma should be removed at the end of the procedure

saqs.q: Describe the correct chair and operator positioning, and the roles of the opposite hand and the assistant.
saqs.a: CHAIR — maxillary: mouth at the dentist's shoulder height, occlusal surface 45° to horizontal; mandibular: lower, near elbow level, occlusal surface parallel to horizontal. OPERATOR — stand erect, force from arm and shoulder; 7 o'clock for all maxillary and most mandibular, 10 o'clock (behind right) for right mandibular posteriors. OPPOSITE HAND — support the alveolus, reflect tissue, support the mandible, protect other teeth, deliver the tooth, compress the socket. ASSISTANT — support head and mandible, aid access and vision, give support, hold suction, protect opposing teeth.

rows: CHAIR — maxillary
the patient's mouth at the same height as the dentist's shoulder, occlusal surface at 45° to the horizontal when open
CHAIR — mandibular
positioned lower, nearly at the level of the dentist's elbow, occlusal surface parallel to the horizontal
OPERATOR POSITION
standing preferred, erect without bending the back, force distributed equally on both legs and delivered from the arm and shoulder rather than the hand alone
WHERE TO STAND

7 o'clock (in front and to the right; to the left for left-handed dentists) for all maxillary teeth and all mandibular except the right posteriors · 10 o'clock (right and behind) for the right mandibular posterior teeth

Assistant

support the head and mandible · help the operator gain access and visualisation · give psychological and emotional support · hold the suction · protect the teeth of the opposite arch
